title: Selection of SC justices in PH and US
primary_topics: Comparison of the PH JBC-based SC appointment system vs the US Senate-confirmation process
The current JBC process: two new PH vacancies, composition, vetting criteria, contentious Congress-representative issue
The US Garland-Gorsuch standoff as a contrast case demonstrating the partisan nature of the US system

JBC composition: CJ as ex officio chair, Secretary of Justice, one Congress representative; Integrated Bar, law professor, retired SC member, private sector representative
Current regular JBC members: Fernan-Cayosa, Mejia, Sandoval-Gutierrez, Ilao Jr.
Congress-representative controversy: split calendar year -- Sen. Gordon (second half 2016), Rep. Umali (first half 2017)

stances.claim: The PH JBC system is superior to the US Senate-confirmation process in three structural ways: it insulates justices from partisan politics by limiting presidential choices to a JBC shortlist, mandates four positive traits (competence, integrity, probity, independence), and imposes a 90-day deadline.
stances.rhetorical_move: three-structural-advantage framing of the PH system
stances.confidence: implied ('You be the judge' withholds explicit endorsement)

stances.claim: The contentious Congress-representative issue -- shifting between half-vote, full-vote, and split-calendar-year arrangements -- reflects an unresolved constitutional ambiguity, with Umali's petition raising legitimate fairness concerns.

The US Senate's one-year refusal to act on Garland's nomination is the most concrete example of partisan capture of judicial selection -- demonstrating exactly the vice the PH JBC system was designed to prevent.
stances.rhetorical_move: negative-exemplar argument (Garland as what PH avoids)

notable_anecdotes: The Republican Senate refusing for an entire year to act on Merrick Garland's nomination -- the most vivid demonstration of US partisan judicial selection.

Rep. Umali's complaint that his first-half-2017 JBC slot missed all four SC vacancies (two in December 2016, two in July-August 2017) -- making his participation purely ceremonial, motivating his SC petition.
Trump's vow to name a 'textualist, originalist, and conservative' -- openly partisan judicial philosophy criteria implicitly contrasted with the JBC's four neutral traits.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban uses the simultaneous SC appointment processes of Duterte (two vacancies from Perez's and Brion's December 2016 retirements) and Trump (Scalia's February 2016 vacancy) to compare the PH JBC system with the US Senate-confirmation process. The PH system -- designed to insulate the Court from partisan politics after the Marcos martial law experience -- limits presidential choices to a JBC shortlist of at least three nominees, mandates four traits (proven competence, integrity, probity, independence), and imposes a 90-day deadline. The JBC composition includes the CJ as ex officio chair, the Secretary of Justice, a Congress representative (currently split: Sen. Gordon for second half 2016, Rep. Umali for first half 2017), plus four regular members (Fernan-Cayosa, Mejia, Sandoval-Gutierrez, Ilao Jr.). Umali filed an SC petition on December 29, 2016 seeking two Congress votes, claiming the Charter was written expecting a unicameral legislature. The US system requires presidential nomination and Senate confirmation -- and lacks a JBC, four-trait mandate, or deadline. The Republican Senate refused to act on Obama's Garland nomination for a full year; Trump vowed to name a 'textualist, originalist, and conservative' within two weeks of his January 20 inauguration. CJ closes: 'Which is the better (or worse) system? You be the judge.'
